newsitem.title: USA: Travel opportunities for wheelchair users, slow walkers.
newsitem.headline: Travel opportunities for wheelchair users, slow walkers.

text.p: The world is opening up for wheelchair users, slow walkers or others who are mobility impaired.

There are few limits to U.S. travel for those who use a wheelchair or crutches, due in part to recent legislation making public buildings, museums, restaurants and restrooms accessible to the physically challenged.
Outside the United States it's a different story, however, since local legislation may not require such modifications.

Yet several tour operators who specialise in travel for those with physical limitations say that with some advance planning, a wheelchair should not keep you from a cruise or a trip to South America, Europe or the Far East.
One could say the theme is, "have money, will travel."

"People are living longer, rehabilitation is wonderful ... people are faster able to re-enter the mainstream. They want recreation and have the dollars to spend on it," said Barbara Jacobson, president of Flying Wheels Travel, in Owatonna, Minn. (800-535-6790).
With her late husband who was a quadriplegic, "we realised the need for this product" and formed Flying Wheels in 1970.

When the Americans with Disasbilities Act (ADA) was passed in 1990, travel in the United States became far more accessible. Ramps were built, and elevators and bathrooms were enlarged to accommodate wheelchairs.

Jacobson said that due to the growing demand for wheelchair accessible travel, cruise lines "have awakened to this market." She said that the newest ships are being built with 10-20 cabins that are wheelchair friendly.
Going ashore, however, is another story. Ports are not always accessible and Jacobson stressed that vacationers should check this out with tour directors or cruise lines before they book their trip.
Flying Wheels' 1997 trips include an eight-day pilgrimage to Fatima, Portugal, ($1,695 plus air fare per person) and a trip to Egypt ($2,225 plus airfare).

Travel outside the United States is not for travelers with very limited funds, because "budget hotels, or anything below two stars, often are not (wheelchair) accessible," said Howard McCoy, a director of Accessible Journeys (800-846-4537; www.disabilitytravel.com).
"Accessible is a relative term," he said, and before deciding if a trip has appropriate facilites, vacationers should ask about hotel rooms, bathrooms, air or land transport and restaurants.
Having a handicap doesn't keep travelers from going to China, India or on African safaris. Accessible Journeys does much of its inland travel by van, even so far as taking travelers through Nepal.
One of the few places in the world that has gotten thumbs down from the company is Russia.
"We were disgusted," McCoy said. "It was very difficult to take a group of wheelchair travelers to Russia." Even Red Square has steps, he said.

As in many tour packages, the prices are all-inclusive. They range at Accessible Journeys from $1,695 per person for a 10-day tour to the U.S. National Parks, to $3,500 for a 12-day tour of Great Britain.
"We try to design (the tours) so prices are the same. To charge more (for disabled travelers) is discrimination," McCoy said.

Currently, there are 100 travel agencies in the United States that specifically serve the disabled traveller, out of more than 33,500 agencies nationwide, according to the American Society of Travel Agents.
However, the ASTA said that 86 percent of its member agents said they have handled special requests from disabled travelers.
Canoeing and rafting trips are a speciality of Wilderness Inquiry (800-728-0719), a non-profit organisation that brings together people of all backgrounds and abilities.

The group sponsors a lot of water-based activities because "it puts people on even ground," said Jennifer MacLeod, outreach director. A person who uses a wheelchair can ride in a white water raft or canoe as well as an able-bodied person.
The mobility impaired need not forgo sledding or snow-shoeing, MacLeod said, joining on such expeditions in a "pulk" sled -- a chair on runners.
Another company, NeverLand Adventures Inc. (800-717-U-CAN) of Cincinnati, Ohio, offers tours of Austraila, scuba holidays and skiing trips "designed by and for challenged travelers."

"One could say that the basic reason disabled people don't travel is fear of the unexpected," said Gary Sharp, director of development at AccessAbility Travel, Cambridge, Mass. (800-610-5640; www.disabled-travel.com).

Fear of poor health is another concern, but McCoy said that travel is generally self-limiting -- people in bad health generally do not go. Just in case, many tours include a nurse among the chaperones. One can travel with a personal aid attendant, but that cost is borne by the traveller.

The Society for the Advancement of Travel for the Handicapped, a non-profit group, has information and fact sheets on travel and various destinations. For membership and general information, write to the society at 347 Fifth Ave., Suite 610, New York, N.Y., 10016. telephone: 212-447-7284, fax: 212-725-8253. Membership is $45 a year, $30 for seniors and students.
You can write to Judith Schoolman at Reuters, 199 Water Street, 10th floor, N.Y., N.Y. 10038. Her e-mail address is Judith.Schoolman(at)reuters.com.
